Title: On Chollet's Permanent Conjecture for Graph Laplacians
Text:
On Chollet’s Permanent Conjecture for Graph Laplacians
Priyanshu Pant
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Indore, India
priyanshupant03@gmail.com
Ranveer Singh
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Indore, India
ranveer@iiti.ac.in
Abstract
In 1982, Chollet conjectured that per(A◦B) ≤per(A) per(B) for Hermitian positive semidefi-
nite matrices A, B, where ◦denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) product, and observed that in the
real symmetric case it suffices to prove per(A◦A) ≤per(A)2. We prove per(A◦A) ≤per(A)2 for
symmetric Z-matrices with nonnegative diagonal whose support graph is bipartite. Motivated
by this, we study the Laplacian inequality per(LG ◦LG) ≤per(LG)2 for the graph Laplacian
LG. We introduce a compositional framework for permanental inequalities on graph Laplacians,
showing that Chollet’s inequality is preserved under vertex coalescence. This enables the ex-
tension of the inequality from basic graph classes to large structured families, revealing new
tractable regimes for a fundamentally #P-hard quantity.
Keywords. Chollet’s conjecture, permanent, graph Laplacian, Hadamard product, positive semidef-
inite matrices, vertex coalescence

In 1982, Chollet [6] proposed the following conjecture.
Conjecture 1.1 (Chollet [6]). If A, B ⪰0 are Hermitian positive semidefinite, then
per(A ◦B) ≤per(A) per(B).
For n ≤3, Conjecture 1.1 was proved by Gregorac–Hentzel [7]. For n = 4, it is known for real
PSD matrices by Hutchinson [10] and for general PSD matrices by Rodtes [18]. For n ≥5, the
conjecture remains open.
Much work on the conjecture focuses on correlation matrices (PSD matrices with diagonal entries
1). In the positive definite case, diagonal scaling reduces to this form, and the inequality is invariant
under such scaling. See Grone–Pierce [8], Zhang [22, 23, 24], and Sa-Nguansin–Rodtes [19]. These
works suggest that structure of the matrix also matters, not only the size. Chollet [6] observed that
it suffices to prove the following inequality: for every Hermitian PSD matrix A ⪰0,
per(A ◦A) ≤| per(A)|2,
where A denotes the entrywise complex conjugate of A; see [6] for the original reduction.
In
particular, in the real symmetric PSD case, A = A, so it suffices to prove
per(A ◦A) ≤per(A)2.
Motivated by this reduction, we study Chollet’s conjecture for the Laplacian matrix LG of a graph
G. Graph Laplacians are real PSD and the structure of G allows a clean interpretation of per(LG)
in terms of cycle covers.
Establishing such inequalities offers rare structural insight into a #P-hard quantity that typically
resists both efficient computation and analysis. In particular, studying how the permanent behaves
under operations such as the Hadamard product can reveal hidden regularities in structured matri-
ces, including graph Laplacians. These inequalities may also be viewed as correlation-type bounds,
with implications for counting problems and probabilistic models on graphs. Moreover, in the set-
ting of graph Laplacians, they naturally connect to combinatorial objects such as cycle covers and
matchings, which play a central role in algorithm design and counting complexity. Consequently,
progress on this conjecture contributes to a deeper understanding of counting problems, quantum
computation, and structural aspects of complexity theory.

Our contributions are as follows.

• We prove the matrix inequality per(A ◦A) ≤per(A)2 for symmetric Z-matrices A = (aij)
(that is, aii ≥0 and aij ≤0 for i ̸= j) whose support graph is bipartite (Theorem 3.1). This
yields (1.1) for all bipartite graphs (Corollary 3.2).
• Let G = G1 · G2 be obtained by identifying v1 ∈V (G1) and v2 ∈V (G2). If (1.1) holds for G1
and G2, and also for the principal submatrices LG1(v1) and LG2(v2), then (1.1) holds for G
(Theorem 4.1).
• We also establish (1.1) for cycles (Theorem 5.1) and for complete graphs (Lemma 5.2). By
iterating the closure theorem, we obtain (1.1) for several additional graph families (Section 5).
Organization.
Section 2 gives the preliminaries related to permanents and PSD matrices. Section 3 proves per(A◦
A) ≤per(A)2 for symmetric Z-matrices whose support graph is bipartite, and derives (1.1) for
bipartite graphs. Section 4 proves the main closure step under vertex coalescence and records two
derived closure operations (leaf attachment and single-edge join), together with a diagonal-closure
lemma. Section 5 collects further graph families covered by iterating these operations; it also states
the cycle and complete-graph cases, with proofs given in Appendices A and B. Finally, Section 6
lists open problems and directions.

A zero-submatrix criterion for permanents.
For (0, 1) matrices, the Frobenius–König theorem says that per(A) = 0 if and only if A contains a
zero submatrix of size r × s with r + s = n + 1; see [3]. For general matrices, we have the following
observation.
Lemma 2.1. Let A = (aij) be an n × n matrix. Suppose A has an r × s submatrix B with all
entries equal to 0, and r + s > n. Then per(A) = 0.
Proof. Let I, J ⊆[n] be the row and column index sets of B, so |I| = r, |J| = s, and aij = 0 for all
i ∈I and j ∈J. By definition,

Nonnegativity of PSD permanents.
We will also use the following standard nonnegativity property of permanents of PSD matrices.
Lemma 2.4 ([17]). If A ⪰0 is Hermitian positive semidefinite, then per(A) ≥0. Consequently,
for every S ⊆[n], the principal submatrix A[S] is also PSD and hence per(A[S]) ≥0.

Proof. Let C be the unique cycle of G. A unicyclic graph is exactly a cycle with (possibly empty)
trees attached to some of its cycle vertices. We start from C and attach these trees. The inequality
holds for the starting cycle C by Theorem 5.1. Each attached tree is bipartite, so the inequality
(and the needed principal-submatrix inequalities) hold for it by Corollary 3.2 and Corollary 3.3.
On the cycle side, deleting any attachment vertex from C leaves a path, hence a bipartite support
graph; therefore the required principal-submatrix inequality for the cycle Laplacian follows from
Theorem 3.1. Thus every attachment step satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 4.1, and iterating
the coalescence closure yields (1.1) for G.
Corollary 5.5 (One-vertex unions). Let H1, . . . , Ht be connected graphs and choose vertices vi ∈
V (Hi). Let G be obtained by taking the disjoint union of the Hi and identifying all vi into a single
vertex (a one-vertex union). Assume for each i that

Proof. Build G by repeated vertex coalescence: start from H1, then glue H2 at v2, then glue H3 at
v3, and so on. At each step, Theorem 4.1 applies: the needed inequalities for the newly added piece
are assumed, and the inequalities for the already constructed graph hold by induction. Hence (1.1)
is preserved at every step, and therefore holds for the final graph G.
The hypotheses in Corollary 5.5 are automatically satisfied when each Hi belongs to one of the
graph families covered earlier (bipartite graphs, cycles, or complete graphs). This includes standard
families such as bouquets (roses) of cycles (one-vertex unions of cycles), windmill graphs (one-vertex
unions of cliques), and friendship graphs (one-vertex unions of copies of triangles). Moreover, we
can combine these building blocks further using the single-edge join closure (Corollary 4.5). In
particular, this covers block graphs, i.e., graphs whose blocks (maximal 2-connected components)
are cliques arranged in a tree-like way via cut vertices.
More generally, it also covers “trees of
blocks” where each block is itself a covered graph (such as a bipartite graph, a cycle, a clique, or a
one-vertex union of these), and the blocks are connected by single-edge joins.
6
Discussion and open problems
We proved (1.1) for several base graph families and showed it is preserved under vertex coalescence
under additional principal-submatrix hypotheses (Theorem 4.1). The methods raise some natural
questions.
• If A ⪰0 is real symmetric and satisfies only per(A ◦A) ≤per(A)2, must the inequality also
hold for A+D for all diagonal matrix D? If not, characterize additional conditions (graphical,
spectral, or combinatorial) that make diagonal closure valid.
• If (1.1) holds for G1 and G2, must it hold for G1 · G2 without assuming the corresponding
inequalities for principal submatrix LG1(v1) and LG2(v2)?
• Our analysis shows that the inequality is strict for odd cycles (Remark A.2). It would be
interesting to characterize graphs G for which equality holds in (1.1), and give lower bounds
on per(LG)2 −per(LG ◦LG) in terms of simple structural parameters like cut vertices/blocks,
the presence and parity of cycles or counts of matchings/cycle-covers.

Abstract: In 1982, Chollet conjectured that per(A◦B) ≤per(A) per(B) for Hermitian positive semidefi- nite matrices A, B, where ◦denotes the Hadamard (entrywise) product, and observed that in the real symmetric case it suffices to prove per(A◦A) ≤per(A)2. We prove per(A◦A) ≤per(A)2 for symmetric Z-matrices with nonnegative diagonal whose support graph is bipartite. Motivated by this, we study the Laplacian inequality per(LG ◦LG) ≤per(LG)2 for the graph Laplacian LG. We introduce a compositional framework for permanental inequalities on graph Laplacians, showing that Chollet’s inequality is preserved under vertex coalescence. This enables the ex- tension of the inequality from basic graph classes to large structured families, revealing new tractable regimes for a fundamentally #P-hard quantity.
